visual.veredicto: Ask: does the chemical form of the carbon change?

turnos.t: Every flow is one of two types, and this will definitely come up.
Ask yourself one question: does the chemical form of the carbon change?
If the carbon just moves from one store to another without changing form, it is a transfer. Example: feeding.
The glucose in the leaf moves into the rabbit, but it is still an organic compound.
The same goes for defecation, for sedimentation, also called burial, and for extraction.
If the chemical form changes, it is a transformation.
Photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide into glucose.
Cellular respiration and combustion do the opposite.
Here is a trick: a transfer moves the box.
A transformation changes what is inside the box.
You already met the two main transformations in unit two point two.
Photosynthesis: six carbon dioxide plus six water, with light energy, gives glucose plus six oxygen.
Cellular respiration is the reverse: glucose plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide, water and energy.
In two point two you were following the energy, which ends up as heat.
Here you are following the carbon, and carbon is never lost: respiration sends it back to the air.
Now the classic trap.
"Extracting coal is a transformation because the coal leaves the lithosphere." False.
Extraction only moves the carbon, so it is a transfer.
The transformation comes later, with combustion.

visual.pie: Net carbon change = carbon inputs − carbon outputs (Codony, T2C3)

turnos.t: The second big idea is the one behind the seven-mark question.
To decide whether something is a sink, a store or a source, you do a subtraction.
The net carbon change equals carbon inputs minus carbon outputs.
What comes in, minus what goes out.
If more comes in than goes out, the answer is positive and it gains carbon: it is a carbon sink.
If the same amount comes in as goes out, the answer is zero: it is a carbon store.
If more goes out than comes in, the answer is negative: it is a carbon source.
The definitions: a carbon sink is a store that takes in more carbon than it releases.
A carbon source is a store that releases more carbon than it takes in.

visual.titulo: Carbon in vs out per year (illustrative units)

turnos.t: Three forests, with example numbers.
First, a young, growing forest.
Eight units come in through photosynthesis, and five go out through respiration and decomposition.
Eight minus five is plus three: a carbon sink.
Second, a mature forest.
Six come in, six go out.
Zero: a carbon store.
It holds a huge amount of carbon, but it is not gaining any more.
Third, a forest that has been burned or cut down.
Two come in, ten go out, through combustion and decomposition.
Minus eight: a carbon source, even though there is still carbon in its soil.
The subtraction decides.
And Codony adds a note with an asterisk: mature forests can still act as sinks, depending on conditions.
Saying that can earn you a mark.

visual.pie: White Cliffs of Dover: chalk, a calcium carbonate limestone. Huge store, very slow sink.

turnos.t: A typical trap is thinking that the biggest store must be the best sink. False.
Look at the White Cliffs of Dover, in England.
They are made of chalk, a soft limestone made of calcium carbonate.
They have held an enormous amount of carbon for millions of years.
But each year they take in very little new carbon.
A gigantic store, but a very slow sink.
Codony puts it like this: large stores need not be fast sinks.
The classification depends on the net exchange, not on how much carbon is stored.
Go back to the bathtub: a full bathtub with the tap almost closed is not filling up quickly.

visual.pie: Fossil fuels = organic carbon. Limestone = inorganic carbon (Codony, T2C3)

turnos.t: The lithosphere is the long-term store, and it holds carbon in two forms.
On the left, fossil fuels.
This is organic carbon: the ancient remains of plants and marine organisms, buried under sediments and changed by heat and pressure, over millions of years, into coal, oil and natural gas.
On the right, limestone.
This is inorganic carbon.
Shells and corals are made of calcium carbonate.
When they are buried and cemented together, they form limestone.
Don't mix them up.
Organic matter gives fossil fuels.
Calcium carbonate gives limestone.
And at the bottom: slow formation, over millions of years; fast release, in decades of combustion.

visual.nota: Plus deforestation: a forest sink or store becomes a source

turnos.t: Why does this matter?
Because humans have sped up one arrow.
Fossil fuels took millions of years to form, and through extraction and combustion we send their carbon back to the air in decades.
Carbon is leaving the slowest store much faster than it went in.
Consequence one: carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, so it strengthens the greenhouse effect.
That is the enhanced greenhouse effect.
Consequence two: part of it dissolves in the ocean, forms carbonic acid and lowers the pH.
That is ocean acidification, and it makes it harder for corals and shellfish to build their calcium carbonate.
And in two point two, Codony mentioned deforestation: cutting down a forest turns it into a source.

escenas.titulo: Recap: the carbon cycle in one picture

turnos.t: Let's put it all together in one picture.
Six stores: the atmosphere, plants and animals, soil, oceans, fossil fuels and sedimentary rock.
Photosynthesis puts carbon into living things, and respiration sends it back.
Decomposition takes it to the soil.
Fossilisation, over millions of years, turns it into fossil fuels.
Extraction and combustion send it back to the air in decades.
On the other side, dissolution carries it into the ocean, and sedimentation locks it away in rock.
Volcanoes also release carbon dioxide.
For every arrow, ask three questions.
From which store to which store does it go?
Is it a transfer or a transformation?
And is it fast or slow?

escenas.titulo: For the exam: energy vs matter

visual.titulo: Distinguish energy flow vs matter cycling [4]

turnos.t: Now, for the exam.
A four-mark question: distinguish between the flow of energy and the cycling of matter in an ecosystem.
Distinguish means contrast.
If you only write "energy flows and matter cycles", you get one mark.
Here are four marks.
One: energy enters as light, and producers convert it into chemical energy.
Two: at each level, energy is lost as heat in respiration, so it must be replaced. Energy flows.
Three: decomposers return nutrients to the soil or the air.
Four: producers take them up again, the very same atoms. Matter cycles.
Another typical question, for six marks: transfers versus transformations.
Give the definition based on chemical form, and two explained examples of each.

visual.titulo: Forest as sink, store or source [7]

pasos.detalle: net change = inputs − outputs, not size
in: photosynthesis; out: respiration, decomposition, combustion
in > out: sink, CO₂ stored as wood
in ≈ out: store (*can stay a sink)

turnos.t: The star question, for seven marks: explain how a forest can act as a carbon sink, a carbon store or a carbon source.
Here is the structure.
First, the rule: it depends on the net carbon change, inputs minus outputs, not on how much carbon it holds.
Second, the processes: carbon comes in through photosynthesis, and goes out through respiration, decomposition and, if it burns, combustion.
Third, a growing forest: inputs are bigger, so it is a carbon sink, sequestering carbon dioxide as wood.
Fourth, a mature forest: inputs roughly equal outputs, so it is a carbon store, although it may still be a sink.
Fifth, a burned or cleared forest: outputs are bigger, so it is a carbon source.
And the four-mark one on fossil fuels: burial, heat and pressure over millions of years; extraction and combustion in decades.

escenas.titulo: The end: review with your notes

visual.texto: Energy flows, matter cycles. Follow the carbon: what comes in, what goes out.

turnos.t: And that brings us to the end of the video: a summary of Topic one, then Topic two in depth, with the carbon cycle at the end.
If you keep just one idea, make it this one: energy flows, matter cycles.
Energy is lost as heat.
Carbon goes round and round, between the air, living things, the soil, the ocean and the rocks.
And the question is always the same: how much comes in, and how much goes out?
Now, review with your notes.
They have the definitions, the tables and the model answers.
Draw the cycle from memory once, say your answers out loud, and get a good rest before Monday. Good luck.
You are going to do really well.
